anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from a static physical-schema/index design that mismatches workload access patterns, relies on stale or insufficient optimizer statistics that distort cost estimates, and is further constrained by saturated or unreliable network/connection resources. Together these three root causes drive inefficient execution paths and unpredictable end-to-end latency that cannot be alleviated by addressing only one layer.

Combined anomalous phenomena: Queries that already scan large tables or perform excessive row fetches because of missing or inappropriate indexes receive plans based on badly misestimated cardinalities, amplifying plan inefficiency (e.g., choosing nested-loop joins with millions of actual rows or avoiding desirable indexes assumed to be non-selective). The bloated I/O and CPU generated by these misguided plans elongate server processing time, which in turn prolongs result streaming across an overloaded network layer. Meanwhile, clients experience longer connection establishment, higher query latency, intermittent timeouts, and sporadic "too many connections" or socket reset errors. Monitoring shows a mixture of symptoms: chronic full-table scans, high logical and physical I/O, optimizer estimated-vs-actual row count ratios far from one, frequent statistics refresh or dynamic sampling events, growing server-side session queues, client-read/client-write waits, retransmissions, and surges in aborted connections during workload spikes.

Causal interaction: Poor schema/index design forces heavier data access, making execution cost and row-count estimates more sensitive to statistics accuracy; when those statistics are stale or lack correlation data, the optimizer consistently selects sub-optimal plans that magnify I/O and CPU demand. The inflated resource usage increases query response time and stretches transaction duration, holding server processes and network sockets open longer. This higher concurrency exacerbates listener queue saturation, connection pool exhaustion, and packet congestion, which feeds back additional latency into application tiers. The ensuing retries or prolonged sessions further raise database load, masking the underlying design and statistics issues and complicating diagnosis. Thus, the three anomalies reinforce each other, creating a feedback loop that degrades both compute efficiency and network-level service quality across OLTP and analytical workloads.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the amount of time after which a TCP keepalive message that has not been acknowledged by the client should be retransmitted.
entry.trigger_condition: A TCP keepalive probe is not acknowledged for tcp_keepalives_interval on systems supporting TCP_KEEPINTVL or an equivalent socket option.
entry.workload_impact: Controls retry timing for keepalive probes used to detect unresponsive client connections.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
